svg.aria-label: Diagram: Azure deny assignments, showing that they are evaluated before role assignments and block access outright, the three things they can do that a role assignment cannot, the fact that customers cannot create them directly and that deployment stack deny settings are the only customer-facing route, the three deny settings modes, and the limits including a maximum of five excluded principals which returns no error when exceeded
svg.title: Deny assignments are the only subtraction in Azure RBAC, and a deployment stack is the only way a customer can create one
svg.text: The only thing in Azure RBAC that subtracts — and you cannot create one directly.
Deny assignments are created and managed by Azure. The one customer-facing route is a deployment stack’s deny settings.
Where it sits in the evaluation, from post #18
Request arrives
token, group memberships
Deny assignments checked
if one applies, access is blocked
Role assignments
Actions − NotActions
Conditions
then allow or deny
Three things a deny assignment does that a role assignment cannot
Exclude principals
Deny everyone except a named few.
The All Principals principal is a zero
GUID with type SystemDefined.
Stop at the scope
DoNotApplyToChildScopes prevents
inheritance downward. Role
assignments always inherit.
Reach classic administrators
Applies to classic subscription
administrator assignments, which
nothing else in RBAC does.
Every deny assignment is currently system protected: created by Azure, and not editable or deletable by you.
The one route you control: a deployment stack’s deny settings
denySettingsMode: none
no deny assignment is created
denySettingsMode: denyDelete
managed resources can be changed but not deleted
denySettingsMode: denyWriteAndDelete
managed resources are frozen to everyone not excluded
excludedActions
up to 200 management operations exempted from the deny
excludedPrincipals
a maximum of five — and more than five returns no error
Exclude Entra groups rather than individuals: membership changes without redeploying the stack.
What the deny setting does not cover
Control plane operations only. A key vault is protected; the secrets inside it are a data plane concern and are not.
Explicitly created resources only. An AKS cluster is managed; the virtual machines it creates to support itself are not in the Bicep file,
so they are implicitly created and fall outside the deny settings entirely.
Where you put the stack decides who can lift the protection
The deny assignment lives where the stack lives. To protect resources in a subscription, place the stack at the parent management group:
the teams working in those resource groups keep write access to their resources and cannot edit the stack that protects them.
Two built-in roles split this: Azure Deployment Stack Contributor manages stacks but cannot create or delete deny assignments within
them; Azure Deployment Stack Owner can. That is the difference between operating a stack and being able to switch it off.
Sources: List Azure deny assignments, deployment stacks in Bicep, Azure Blueprints overview, and Azure subscription and service limits, on Microsoft Learn.
